splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA's statutory measurement date for withdrawal liability requires all actuarial assumptions to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries retain discretion to select assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be established by the statutory measurement date (end of prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that plan actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the date fixes only the financial data to be measured, not the professional judgments applied to that data.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled while a supervisee is a fugitive, so the supervision period is extended by the time spent absconding.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release runs continuously and is not tolled by absconding, because no statute authorizes such tolling and judicial creation of the doctrine exceeds courts' authority.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive collateral attack, in addition to the separate requirements in § 2255(h). This determines whether federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim previously presented.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions; they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can demonstrate sufficient injury-in-fact to challenge election administration rules before an election takes place. The outcome affects whether pre-election challenges to voting procedures are viable or must wait until after the election, raising practical concerns about timeliness of judicial review.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for office have Article III standing to challenge state election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes or affect election integrity, based on competitive injury.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules because they cannot show concrete and particularized injury traceable to the challenged law.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps Auer/Kisor deference to agency interpretations when construing ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines that increase criminal penalties.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions that expand criminal liability, or whether the rule of lenity should take precedence. The Third Circuit holds that deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference in criminal contexts.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor deference when construing ambiguous Sentencing Guidelines provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary prevails over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions, even those that increase criminal penalties.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief under § 3553(f)(1) only if they meet all three listed criminal-history criteria, or if possessing any one of them is disqualifying. This directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses and creates geographic sentencing disparities.

positions.label: 'And' means conjunctive — all three required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' conjunctively.

positions.label: 'And' means disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' based on context and statutory structure.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1 to the commentary, or whether the text unambiguously excludes them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' for the career-offender enhancement, is a valid authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor. The split affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is valid and inchoate offenses are included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and that conspiracy and other inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Application Note 1 exceeds guideline text and inchoate offenses are excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline's scope beyond its plain meaning.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) when the state's drug schedules are broader than the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires a match with federal drug schedules or encompasses any offense under state law, even if the state criminalizes substances not controlled under federal law. This directly affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: State law controls — no federal schedule match required
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law regardless of whether the substance is federally controlled, because there is no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal schedule match required
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, applying the categorical approach.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit categorically bars such consideration, while the Seventh Circuit (via the Sentencing Commission's amended policy statement in § 1B1.13(b)(6)) has addressed whether the Commission can override circuit precedent on this point. Other circuits have allowed consideration of non-retroactive changes as part of the totality of circumstances.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be extraordinary and compelling
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered as part of the totality of circumstances when evaluating extraordinary and compelling reasons, and that the Sentencing Commission's policy statement in § 1B1.13(b)(6) allows such consideration.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly consider the need to punish a defendant when revoking supervised release and imposing a revocation sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether punishment is a permissible consideration at supervised release revocation. The Sixth Circuit allows courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at the 'extreme' end of the split, while other circuits have held that the statutory factors for revocation do not include punishment as an independent sentencing purpose.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider punishment as a purpose when revoking supervised release and imposing a sentence upon revocation.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that the statutory framework for supervised release revocation does not authorize courts to impose sentences for the purpose of punishment, as Congress excluded 'just punishment' from the applicable sentencing factors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the duration of their custody (such as First Step Act time-credit denials) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims.
splits.description: Circuits have developed an unresolved, longstanding conflict over whether challenges to BOP decisions regarding earned time credits, prerelease custody transfers, and similar matters affecting the duration of confinement must be brought as habeas petitions or may be pursued through civil rights actions. The Supreme Court has noted but not resolved this issue since Preiser v. Rodriguez (1973).

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the fact or duration of confinement, including First Step Act time-credit disputes, must be brought exclusively through habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241.

positions.label: Civil rights claims also available
positions.summary: Holds that some challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions may be brought through civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens or § 1983) even when they arguably affect the duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appellate deadline applies to appeals from orders on Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day civil deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering the 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtors. The Ninth Circuit holds that such appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a split with circuits that hold it belongs to the debtors based on the statute's structure and legislative history.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with the broad scope of § 541(a)'s definition of estate property, means that post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtors
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors who converted in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the denial of a motion to seal medical records in litigation qualifies as an immediately appealable collateral order. The D.C. Circuit holds that medical privacy is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, while other circuits have reached different conclusions on the applicability of the collateral order doctrine to sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that warrants immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine, because such privacy rights are effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are generally not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as the interest in sealing can be adequately vindicated through other means such as protective orders or post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
